01 / COURSE EDIT

Why you will not do all 34 units

This plan picks the parts you can build and enjoy right now. You can learn the harder tools when you need them.

Learn these now

These units move from drawing to choices, loops, controls, and games.

U1 Start + turtleU2 VariablesU3 Math + booleansU4 ifU6 LoopsU7 FunctionsU9 EventsU10 Built-in functionsU11 StringsU33 Game basicsU34 Snake

Save these for later

You do not need these harder ideas to build your first game.

U5 match-caseU8 lambdaU13 List shortcutsU17–20 Advanced OOPU21 Recursion + choicesU22–32 Tools + APIs + tests
A bridge to Snake

Unit 34 uses classes and lists. A parent can give you those ready-made parts. You will find and change the parts you know, such as movement, color, speed, and crashes. You do not need to understand every line before you build the game.

03 / EVERY SESSION

Use the same 4 steps every time

A familiar routine saves your energy for coding. Writing by hand and guessing the result first also builds the same good habit you use in math.

Guess on paper

Write the key 3–8 lines by hand. Draw or say where the turtle will go and how far it will move.

Run small pieces

Save and run every 3–5 lines. Do not type the whole program at once.

Read the error

Read the last line, the error name, the line number, and the line above it. Fix one thing. Run again.

Change one thing

When it works, change one color, number, or shape. Guess what will happen first.

5–8 min Paper guess
18–25 min Build
5–8 min Debug
5 min Change + explain
04 / SELF-RUNNING

A learning plan you can run yourself

Use the same steps, timer, and hint cards each time. They will show you what to do next. A parent can practice the routine with you for two weeks. After that, the parent only helps you start and listens at the end.

Your 35-minute desk card

Keep the steps in this order. The work takes 33 minutes. You have 2 extra minutes to clean up. Pick just one goal today.

  1. Start · 3 minSet a 35-minute timer → open your last file → run it once.
  2. Today’s mission · 5 minOn paper, write one thing you will change today. Draw or write what you think will happen.
  3. Build · 20 minSave and run every 3–5 lines. Stuck? Run again → read the last error line → check your last code → use Hint 1, then Hint 2. After 10 minutes, write a Stuck Note. Then try a different experiment you can do alone.
  4. Finish · 5 minSave your file → mark one thing you learned → show a parent your result and Stuck Note.

How a parent steps back

The goal is not a fast answer. The goal is to learn how to ask for help.

WEEK 1

Sit nearby. Help only with saving, running, and closing the window. Do not type the code for Alex.

WEEK 2

Stay in the same room but sit farther away. Answer a question only after Alex checks the desk card.

WEEK 3–8

Check the timer at the start. Join a 5-minute show-and-tell at the end. Alex should work alone in the middle.

When a parent can help right away
Help with setup, a lost file, or an app that will not open. You can also help after Alex has tried for 10 minutes and written a Stuck Note. Ask one question, then step away again.

Weekly hint cards

Look here only after you make a guess and run the code once. Try Hint 1 first. Read Hint 2 only if you are still stuck.

WEEK 01
Save the file. Then press the Run button.forward controls distance. right controls the turn angle.

WEEK 03

Stuck Note

Instead of calling out “It does not work,” write what you know so far. These four lines help you ask a clear question.

What I tried to do
What happened
Last line of the error
Two things I tried
04 / SELF-RUNNING

A learning system Alex can run himself

Instead of teaching each step, use the same sequence, timer, and hint cards to guide Alex toward the next action. Parents learn the routine with him for the first two weeks, then join only for the start and the final show-and-tell.

The 35-minute desk card

Keep the order the same every time. The routine takes 33 minutes, with two extra minutes to put things away. Choose only one goal for the day.

  1. Start · 3 minSet a 35-minute timer → open yesterday’s file → run it once.
  2. Today’s mission · 5 minOn paper, write “one thing I will change today” and predict the result with a drawing or one sentence.
  3. Build · 20 minSave and run every 3–5 lines. If stuck: run again → read the last line of the error → compare with yesterday’s code → use Hint 1, then Hint 2. After 10 minutes on the same problem, write a Stuck Note and move to an experiment you can do on your own.
  4. Finish · 5 minSave the file → mark one thing you learned → briefly show a parent the result and your Stuck Note.

The parent’s three-step fade-out

The goal is not to give the answer quickly. It is to teach a reliable way to ask for help.

WEEK 1

Sit nearby and help only with saving, running, and closing the window. The parent does not type the code.

WEEK 2

Stay elsewhere in the same room. Take a question only after Alex checks the desk card first.

WEEK 3–8

Check the timer at the start and join a five-minute show-and-tell at the end. The default is no calls for help in the middle.

When immediate help is okay
Step in for installation trouble, a lost file, an app that will not open, or after Alex has tried for 10 minutes and completed a Stuck Note. Even then, ask only one question and step away again.

Weekly hint cards

Read these only after making a prediction and running the code once. Try again after Hint 1; read Hint 2 only if you are still stuck.

WEEK 01
Save the file, then press the Run button.forward controls distance; right controls the turning angle.
WEEK 02
Change only one variable at a time and compare before and after.A regular polygon turns 360 / sides degrees each time.
WEEK 03
Turn the first line of your paper rule chart into an if statement.else covers everything that did not match the earlier conditions.
WEEK 04
Put just one shape inside the loop and run it first.After drawing the shape, turn a small extra angle to spread the pattern like a flower.
WEEK 05
Find the lines that appear more than once and move them into a function.Receive size inside the parentheses and use it where the distance goes.
WEEK 06
Connect one movement function to each key.Check that the onkey() connections come after listen().
WEEK 07
Check one step at a time: move → check the star → refresh the screen.If collision detection is hard, print the distance value on screen first.
WEEK 08
Run the completed code unchanged first to establish a working baseline.Change only one of these at a time—color, speed, or score—then run it again.

Stuck Note

Instead of calling “It doesn’t work,” record what you have figured out so far. These four lines prepare a clear question for a parent.

What I tried to do
What actually happened
Last line of the error
Two things I already tried
05 / DEBUGGING

How to read an error

An error is a clue from the computer. It does not mean you failed. Read the clue out loud before a parent gives an answer.

01 · Missing parenthesist.forward(100 → Check for the closing )
02 · Missing quotet.color("blue) → Check that the quote marks match.
03 · Name typo / NameErrorturtel.forward(100) → Check that the spelling matches the name you made.
04 · Indentation / IndentationErrorfor → Check that the commands below it start at the same space.
05 · Turtle window is still openClose the old turtle window. Then run again. The program keeps running while the window is open.

Try these steps

  1. Read the last line of the message
  2. Find the error type
  3. Check the line number and the line above it
  4. Change one thing
  5. Save and run again
06 / WORDS

Coding words

You do not need to memorize these words. Use this list when you see one in your code.

programA set of instructions for a computer
variableA named box that holds a value
data typeThe kind of value, such as text or a number
booleanA value that is only True or False
if statementCode that makes a choice
loopCode that repeats
functionA named group of steps you can reuse
parameterA value you give to a function
eventSomething that happens, such as a key press
stringText inside quote marks
listA group of values kept in order
inputInformation sent into a program
outputWhat a program shows or does
errorA clue that something went wrong
debugFinding and fixing a problem in code
collisionWhen two game objects touch
07 / PARENT GUIDE

Parents: ask instead of telling

Waiting is part of learning. Help Alex think instead of fixing the code for him.

Questions to ask

  • “What do you think the turtle will do?”
  • “Can you trace the loop with your finger?”
  • “What does the last line of the error say?”
  • “What looks different on that line and the line above it?”
  • “What is one thing you could change?”
  • “Can you teach this part to me?”

Four things to avoid

  • Taking the keyboard — Point or ask a question instead.
  • Giving a long lesson — Say one sentence that helps with this code.
  • Copying all the finished code — Guess and run 3–5 lines at a time.
  • Only watching a video — Change the code by hand after watching.
The goal is not to get unstuck fast. The goal is to remember how you solved it.
SEASON 2

After 8 weeks, level up your game

Next season, add new features to your Snake game. You will learn collections while you build.

  1. Unit 12 Use lists for food, walls, and scores
  2. Unit 14–16 Use ranges, tuples, and dictionaries for level rules
  3. Add a feature you choose: a scoreboard, speed levels, walls, or a high score
